newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists may try to impeach Yeltsin for Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Communists may try to impeach Yeltsin for Chechnya.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's communist opponents in parliament said on Monday they may try to impeach him for withdrawing all remaining Russian troops from Chechnya and for Moscow's accord with the region's separatists.
Impeachment moves have failed before and any new bid to oust him stands little chance of success under a constitution Yeltsin himself drew up to concentrate power in the presidency.

It marks an escalation of a row that broke out over the weekend after the Kremlin revealed new concessions to the Chechen rebels which were effectively a recognition of Moscow's utter military defeat after nearly two years of war.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, while insisting he wanted no resumption of hostilities, accused Yeltsin of treason and his Kremlin entourage of scheming behind parliament's back to break up Russia in the same way as the Soviet Union shattered in 1991.

The accord, signed on Saturday by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Chechen government leader Aslan Maskhadov, the man who led the guerrillas to victory over Moscow's regular troops, was a "malignant tumour", Zyuganov said on Sunday.

The communist chairman of parliament's security committee told reporters an emergency debate on the Chechen deal, called at communist insistence for next Friday, should discuss impeachment and a vote of no confidence in the government.

"The deputies are not going to limit themselves to generating hot air," Viktor Ilyukhin said of next Friday's debate in the lower house. "I think the questions of impeachment and of confidence in the government will be raised."
Ilyukhin told Reuters Yeltsin's policy in Chechnya had not just been a "mistake" but a "crime for which he must answer".

Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma, was more cautious, saying the lower house would consider over the next few days whether the accords breached the constitution, notably by giving in to Chechen demands for independence.
If there had been a constitutional fault, then the question of impeachment could be raised on Friday, the speaker said.

It is unlikely to get far, however. Impeachment requires two-thirds majorities in both chambers of parliament and the approval of both the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court -- all within a time limit of three months.
The Duma also has little power to oust Chernomyrdin and the government against Yeltsin's wishes.
The communists are backed by Vladimir Zhirinovsky's hardline nationalists in the Duma. Both groups are incensed at anything that smacks of capitulation to the North Caucasus guerrillas.

The Kremlin remains officially hostile to the Chechens' demands for outright secession. In an initial peace in August both sides agreed to disagree and to leave the final question of Chechnya's sovereign status unresolved for five years.

But Moscow, whose troops were routed last August when Maskhadov's forces seized the Chechen capital Grozny in a daring lighting raid, seems to have recognised it has nothing to gain by taking an aggressive line against the separatists.
Yeltsin, who will spend another two or three weeks at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow convalescing from his november 5 heart operation, made no comment on the Duma's move.
Chernomyrdin discussed the Chechen deal with the president during a 90-minute meeting on Monday before heading for Paris.
